identification.summary: Worok is a cyberespionage group that ESET Research named and publicly described in September 2022 [S1]. ESET says the group has been active since at least 2020 and was still operating at the time of reporting [S1][S2]. Its toolset includes a C++ loader (CLRLoad), a PowerShell backdoor (PowHeartBeat) and a C# loader (PNGLoad) that extracts payloads hidden by steganography in PNG files [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: ESET: active since at least 2020, with operations paused from May 2021 to January 2022 and resuming in February 2022 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Worok is an ESET name; no Microsoft name or MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found in the sources gathered. ESET assessed possible ties to TA428 (a separate tracked cluster) with low confidence only; do not merge the two [S1][S3]. Avast later analysed the DropBoxControl payload tied to the same PNG-loader chain and judged that the author of CLRLoader/PNGLoader did not write DropBoxControl [S5].

attribution.confidence: ESET stated that activity times and toolset indicate possible ties with TA428, an assessment made with low confidence [S3]. No source gathered attributes Worok to a specific government or agency.
attribution.basis: ESET reasoning rests on overlapping activity times and toolset with TA428 [S3]. ESET assessed the group's goal as information theft, based on the victim set [S1][S2]. The original ESET report was not opened directly; this is drawn from coverage of it.

objectives: ESET assesses that the operators are mainly interested in stealing information from high-profile victims, with an emphasis on government entities [S1][S2][S3].

regions: Cambodia, Vietnam and Mexico (Avast, via secondary coverage of DropBoxControl victims)
targeting.notes: ESET: 2020 victims included a telecommunications company in East Asia, a bank in Central Asia, a maritime industry company in Southeast Asia, a government entity in the Middle East and a private company in southern Africa; after the February 2022 resumption, victims included an energy company in Central Asia and a public-sector entity in Southeast Asia [S2][S3][S4]. Avast reportedly saw DropBoxControl affect companies and government agencies in Cambodia, Vietnam, Mexico and other countries [S6].

capabilities.summary: Worok uses custom malware alongside publicly available tools. In 2021 the chain used the CLRLoad loader, which fetches the C# PNGLoad loader; in 2022 CLRLoad was replaced by the full-featured PowerShell backdoor PowHeartBeat, which launches PNGLoad [S2][S3]. PNGLoad extracts hidden payloads from PNG files using steganography; Avast describes least-significant-bit (LSB) encoding of code fragments in pixel data [S1][S5][S6]. ESET did not recover the final payloads from its telemetry [S3]. Avast identified a third-stage .NET C# payload, DropBoxControl, which uses a Dropbox account for command and control and can run executables, upload and download files, delete and rename files, and gather system and network information [S5][S6]. Initial access in some cases was via ProxyShell vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange, followed by web shell deployment for persistence; Avast stated the initial vector in its cases was unclear [S2][S5]. Reconnaissance and post-exploitation tools reported by ESET include Mimikatz, EarthWorm, ReGeorg and NBTscan [S2]. Loaders are believed to be executed via DLL sideloading [S5].

campaigns.name: Initial observed intrusions
campaigns.summary: ESET telemetry shows Worok targeting a telecommunications company in East Asia, a bank in Central Asia, a maritime industry company in Southeast Asia, a Middle East government entity and a private company in southern Africa [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Activity pause
campaigns.summary: ESET observed no operations from May 2021 to January 2022; CLRLoad was the first-stage loader in 2021 [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Resumption with PowHeartBeat
campaigns.summary: Operations resumed in February 2022 against an energy company in Central Asia and a public-sector entity in Southeast Asia, with PowHeartBeat replacing CLRLoad; ProxyShell was exploited in some cases [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: ESET public disclosure
campaigns.summary: ESET published 'Worok: The big picture' and named the group, noting low-confidence ties to TA428 [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: Avast analysis of DropBoxControl
campaigns.summary: Avast reported PNG files carrying a data-stealing payload and the Dropbox-controlled .NET backdoor DropBoxControl; victims reportedly included entities in Cambodia, Vietnam and Mexico [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed to a named government; ESET notes possible, low-confidence ties to TA428 [S3].
diamond.capability: Custom loaders (CLRLoad, PNGLoad), PowerShell backdoor PowHeartBeat, DropBoxControl, steganography in PNG files, ProxyShell exploitation and web shells, plus public tools such as Mimikatz and EarthWorm [S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Dropbox accounts used as C2 for DropBoxControl [S5][S6]; web shells on compromised Exchange servers [S2]. Other C2 details not confirmed in sources gathered.
diamond.victim: High-profile telecom, banking, maritime, energy, government and public-sector organizations in Asia, the Middle East and Africa [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Information theft with a government-information emphasis, per ESET [S1][S2]. State sponsorship is not established in the sources gathered.
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers (ProxyShell) and trusted cloud services (Dropbox) that blend C2 traffic with normal use [S2][S5].

gaps: Sponsor is unknown; only a low-confidence TA428 link from ESET exists [S3].
Final payloads in the ESET-observed PowHeartBeat/PNGLoad chain were not recovered [S3].
ESET's original report (welivesecurity.com) and Avast's original blog could not be opened; findings rely on press coverage of both. Verify against the primary documents.
Initial access outside the ProxyShell cases is unknown [S5].
A secondary article mentions one DropBoxControl connection from an IP linked to a Russian ministry; this was not verified and is omitted from the profile.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft Threat Intelligence name was found. Activity after 2022 was not located in searches run.
Whether the DropBoxControl author is the same actor as the CLRLoad/PNGLoad author is unresolved; Avast judged them different developers [S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing Microsoft Exchange servers, telecom, government and energy networks, and cloud storage egress are key terrain [S2][S3]. STEP 2: Vulnerable, unpatched Exchange (ProxyShell) and allowance of Dropbox traffic widen the operating environment for the adversary [S2][S5]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is ProxyShell or unknown access, web shell, DLL sideloaded CLRLoad/PowHeartBeat, PNGLoad steganographic payload extraction, then Dropbox-based backdoor and data theft [S2][S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume espionage against government, telecom and energy targets in Asia and neighboring regions. MDCOA is use of the same loader chain against allied or partner government networks with ProxyShell-like access, exfiltrating through cloud storage. Candidate indicators: new web shells on Exchange, sideloaded DLLs loading .NET assemblies, PowerShell spawning from Exchange, image files read then decoded in memory, and unexpected Dropbox API calls from servers [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Exchange patch status and cloud-storage egress on mission-relevant networks; the ESET-observed victim set indicates partner-nation and telecom exposure [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: monitoring or blocking cloud-service C2 and sharing indicators with partners requires coordination under the appropriate cyber authorities. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize hardening and logging of internet-facing mail servers on key cyber terrain [S2]. (4) Coordination: attribution is unresolved, so share technical indicators with partners and vendors rather than naming a sponsor [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Worok is a cyber espionage group, mostly targeting Central Asia. The group toolset includes a C++ loader named CLRLoad, a PowerShell backdoor named PowHeartBeat, and a C# loader named PNGLoad.
